identity.plain_name: The basic way to make something turn: a pin, bolt or shaft through a hole, either rubbing straight on the hole (or on a slippery sleeve pushed into it), or running in a ball bearing, a ring with steel balls inside, so it spins more easily
identity.term: Revolute joint (pin joint) made with a plain bearing (pin in a hole or bushing, shoulder bolt) or a rolling-element bearing (ball bearing)
aliases: pin joint, hinge joint, turning pair (revolute joint; Wikipedia)
plain bearing, sliding bearing, sleeve bearing, journal bearing, friction bearing ('simply a shaft rotating in a hole'; Wikipedia)
bush or bushing, flanged bushing, split bushing; thrust washer (the flat version that takes end thrust) (Wikipedia, Plain bearing)
oil-impregnated sintered bronze bushing, SAE 841 bronze, Oilite (brand) (Wikipedia)
self-lubricating plastic bushing; iglidur and iglide (igus brands)
shoulder bolt, shoulder screw, stripper bolt (Machine Design)
rolling-element bearing, rolling bearing, anti-friction bearing (Wikipedia; I Dig Hardware uses 'antifriction bearing')
ball bearing, deep-groove ball bearing, Conrad bearing (the usual construction; Wikipedia)
608 bearing or skateboard bearing (8 mm bore, 22 mm outside, 7 mm wide; Wikipedia, 123bearing)
2Z (metal shields on both sides; 123bearing) and 2RS (rubber seals on both sides; Commons drawing description) bearing suffixes; ZZ is another common shield suffix [uncertain]
pillow block (a housing that holds a bushing or bearing; GM0)
live axle (the shaft turns with the part and is held in bearings; GM0) and dead axle (the part turns on a fixed shaft) [uncertain]
identity.one_liner: A pin or shaft passes through a hole so one part can turn on the other, sliding directly in the hole or a sleeve (plain bearing), or rolling on balls between two rings (ball bearing) for less friction.
identity.complexity: A few parts for a plain pivot: a pin, bolt or shaft, the hole it turns in (often lined with a bushing), and something to stop it sliding out (a head and nut, a shoulder, a retaining ring or a shaft collar), usually with washers. A ball bearing is a small assembly that acts as one unit: inner ring, outer ring, balls, a cage that keeps them spaced, grease, and often shields or seals (Wikipedia, Rolling-element bearing and Ball bearing).
identity.how_it_works: In a plain pivot the pin simply turns in the hole, sliding on its surface. The pin must be a little smaller than the hole to move, so it really touches along a line, and friction and wear depend on the two materials and on lubrication (Wikipedia, Revolute joint and Plain bearing). Pairing a hard, smooth pin with a softer, slippery sleeve (bronze, oil-filled sintered bronze, or a plastic such as nylon or acetal) makes it run smoothly and puts the wear on the cheap sleeve, which is replaced when worn (Wikipedia, Plain bearing). A ball bearing swaps sliding for rolling: balls roll between grooved inner and outer rings, so friction is much lower (Wikipedia, Rolling-element bearing; GM0). The ring that turns relative to the load is fitted tight on its shaft or in its housing so it can't slip round, and the other ring is a looser fit (NSK). The simplest bearing for a push along the pin (end float) is a thrust washer, the flat 'thrust form' of a bushing (Wikipedia, Plain bearing): a ring of metal such as bronze, or of plastic such as nylon or PTFE, between the turning part and the fixed face beside it, used where a rolling thrust bearing isn't worth its cost or won't fit (Wikipedia, Washer (hardware)).

job: let it move (turn, slide or bend): lets a lever, arm, wheel, pulley or shaft turn
join and hold: holds the turning part in place on its support, taking the load across the pin
finder_attributes.motion: rotate: unlimited continuous turning (wheels, shafts, spools) or any part of a turn (levers, arms, linkages). A loose pin in a plain hole can also slide along its length unless a head, shoulder, collar or retaining ring stops it (rotate+slide).
finder_attributes.degrees_of_freedom: 1 when the pin or shaft is held at both ends along its length: turning about its axis (Wikipedia, Revolute joint). A loose pin in a hole also lets the part slide along the pin (2) and wobble through the clearance. A single ball bearing allows a little tilt (Wikipedia, Ball bearing), so a shaft is normally held by two bearings spaced apart.
special_behaviour: none: it just lets parts turn, with less friction when a ball bearing is used
self-aligning or self-centring: only special self-aligning ball bearings, whose outer ring has a spherical track, tolerate a shaft that is not quite in line (Wikipedia, Ball bearing)
holding_principle: not a holding joint (it moves or passes on motion): it lets parts turn

shape (the parts interlock; form-fit): the pin through the hole stops every movement except turning; a head, nut, shoulder, collar or retaining ring stops it sliding out (GM0: retain the shaft in both directions)
friction or clamping (force-fit): bearings and bushings are usually held by a press (interference) fit (NSK; igus)
finder_attributes.input_output: not applicable: a pivot or bearing supports a turning part rather than changing motion. A shaft running in bearings passes rotation straight along itself (in line, 1:1). Ball bearings waste less energy than bushings (GM0).
finder_attributes.removability: removable: pull the pin or undo the bolt or shoulder screw; pressed-in bushings and bearings are harder to remove and may be damaged when pressed out
finder_attributes.reuse_cycles: many times: pins, bolts and shoulder screws can be taken out and put back many times; press-fitted bearings and bushings in printed parts only a few times, since each press wears the fit [uncertain]
finder_attributes.tools_needed: Hex key or spanner for a bolt or shoulder screw; circlip pliers for retaining rings; a vice, arbor press or clamp with a flat punch to press in bushings and bearings (igus: use a flat press, not a centring pin); a drill or reamer to bring printed holes to size (Hubs). None for a pin held by a clip.
finder_attributes.seal: none: a pin in a hole does not seal. Bearings come with metal shields (2Z) or rubber seals (2RS) that keep dirt out of the bearing itself and hold its grease in; seals add friction (Wikipedia, Rolling-element bearing)
finder_attributes.load: Light to heavy, depending on size and material. Plain bearings are the cheapest, most compact type and carry high loads for their size (Wikipedia, Plain bearing). A 608-2Z ball bearing is rated 3.45 kN dynamic and 1.37 kN static (SKF data via 123bearing). Strongest across the pin or shaft (radial load); deep-groove ball bearings also take some push along the shaft, about 50% of their radial rating, or 25% for small or light bearings (Wikipedia, citing SKF). Weak against tipping loads on a single bearing: a sideways twist can distort the outer ring until the balls escape (Wikipedia, Ball bearing), so use two bearings spaced apart. In printed parts the plastic around the hole usually wears or creeps before a metal pin fails [uncertain].
finder_attributes.adjustable: No for a basic pivot. End float is set with washers or shims; a pair of ball bearings can be preloaded against each other to take out their internal play (Wikipedia, Ball bearing). Eccentric bushings let a pivot's position be adjusted (see Eccentric adjuster).
finder_attributes.play_and_precision: Plain pivot: small to noticeable play, because the clearance needed for movement means the pin only touches along a line (Wikipedia, Revolute joint); printed pins in printed holes need at least 0.3 mm clearance (Prusa) and so wobble noticeably, while precision shoulder screws are made 0.013 to 0.038 mm under size for a close but free fit in bearings and pulleys (Machine Design). Ball bearing: small play that can be removed by preloading a pair (Wikipedia), good repeatability, and some tolerance of misalignment (Wikipedia, Ball bearing), though self-aligning types are needed for more.
finder_attributes.access_needed: both sides for a through-bolt with a nut; one side only (blind) for a shoulder screw or bolt screwed into a tapped hole or threaded insert; end of a tube or shaft for sliding a bearing, bushing, collar or retaining ring onto a shaft.
finder_attributes.materials: Pins and shafts: steel, hardened and polished to run in bushings, or stainless steel (Wikipedia, Plain bearing). Bushings: bronze, oil-impregnated sintered bronze (SAE 841 / Oilite), cast iron, graphite, and plastics such as nylon, acetal, PTFE, UHMWPE and PEEK (Wikipedia, Plain bearing); even self-lubricating wood (lignum vitae) in clocks (Wikipedia). Ball bearings: chrome steel (608-2Z; 123bearing), stainless steel or plastic. Printed housings in PLA, PETG, ASA or wear-resistant 'tribo' filaments (igus claims up to 50 times the abrasion resistance of ordinary filament). Joins almost anything.
finder_attributes.maker_difficulty: easy: a bolt through a drilled hole, or a ball bearing pressed into a printed pocket, is one of the first mechanisms most makers build; getting a snug bearing press fit in a print usually takes one or two test prints (Hackaday; Printables 1293573).

processes: off-the-shelf part: ball bearings (608 and other ISO 15 sizes), bushings, thrust washers, shoulder screws, dowel pins, shafts, collars, retaining rings
3D print (FDM): printed housings with pressed-in bearings or bushings and metal pins, or fully printed bearings and bushings (Printables 276409, 693434)
CNC: machined holes, shafts and bearing seats for accurate fits
woodwork: dowel or bolt pivots in wood; piano keys pivot on centre pins in felt bushings (Wikipedia, Plain bearing)
laser cut: pivot holes in plywood or acrylic with a bolt or shoulder screw as the pin [uncertain]
3D print (resin): pivot holes and bearing pockets in resin parts [uncertain]
making.print_in_place: partly: most printed pivots are a printed part plus an added bolt, pin, bushing or ball bearing. Whole 608-size bearings can be printed in place after calibrating two tolerances (Printables 276409; Hackaday), and ball-less printed bushings print as one piece and are squeezed free with pliers (Printables 693434).
making.making_tips_3d_printing: 1) Use metal for the pin: printed pins under 5 mm are weak, so insert an off-the-shelf pin into a drilled hole (Hubs). If a bolt is the pin, let its smooth shank, not its threads, sit in the hole; threads in the hole cause fretting wear (Wikipedia, Bolt). A shoulder screw is made for this: its shoulder is the pivot and the thread clamps it down (Machine Design). 2) Hole size: holes printed upright come out undersized, so print them slightly small and drill or ream to size (Hubs); for parts that move, start with at least 0.3 mm clearance (Prusa). 3) Bearing pockets: a 0.1 mm difference noticeably changes a press fit (Hackaday); crush ribs, small ridges inside the pocket that squash as the bearing goes in, make the fit far more forgiving (Hackaday). Print a quick tolerance tester at your final settings and scale up or down in 0.1 mm steps (Printables 1293573). To trap a bearing inside a part, see Mid-print embedding. 4) Printed bearings: calibrate the radial and 'tenon' tolerances by halving the range each test (binary search); the designer got the best results in PLA at 0.16 mm layers with grease, and warns against filling the bed with copies, which prints differently from one part (Hackaday; Printables 276409). 5) Hold the shaft in both directions, with a washer that touches only the bearing's inner ring so nothing rubs (GM0). 6) Use two bearings spaced apart for any shaft or arm with a sideways load; one bearing can be wrecked by tipping (Wikipedia, Ball bearing). 7) Lubricate printed bushings with a plastic-safe grease or spray such as PTFE or silicone (Hackaday; Printables 693434), or print sliding parts in a wear-resistant filament (igus, manufacturer's claim). 8) Heat: PLA starts to give at about 60 °C and PETG at about 80 °C (CNC Kitchen), and a fast plain printed pivot warms up from friction [uncertain], so use PETG, ASA or a real bushing for continuous rotation.
making.off_the_shelf_parts: Search for: '608-2Z' or '608-2RS' (8 x 22 x 7 mm), other deep-groove ball bearings by ISO 15 number, 'flanged ball bearing' [uncertain], 'sleeve bearing' or 'bushing', 'flanged bushing', 'oil-embedded' or 'sintered bronze bushing' (SAE 841), 'plastic plain bearing' (iglidur, brand), 'thrust washer', 'shoulder screw' or 'shoulder bolt' (ASME B18.3 inch, B18.3.3M metric; 6 to 24 mm commercial shoulders; Machine Design), 'precision shoulder screw', 'dowel pin', 'clevis pin', 'shaft collar' (clamping or set-screw), 'retaining ring' or 'E-clip', 'pillow block' (GM0), 'shim washer'.
rules_of_thumb: Pick a bushing material by PV (pressure on the projected area x sliding speed): maximum PV about 1.75 MPa·m/s for SAE 841 oil-impregnated bronze, 0.11 for nylon, 0.09 for acetal and 0.04 for plain PTFE (Wikipedia, Plain bearing, from McMaster-Carr catalogue data).
Plastic plain bearings (igus): housing hole H7, shaft at least h9, press-fit oversize up to 2% of the inside diameter; press in with a flat punch, not a centring pin (igus iglidur tolerances).
Deep-groove ball bearings take axial (end) loads of about 50% of their radial rating, or 25% for small or light bearings (Wikipedia, Ball bearing, citing SKF).

Tight fit on the ring that turns relative to the load, looser fit on the other ring; too loose and the ring creeps round in its seat, too tight and it can crack or lose its internal clearance and overheat (NSK).
608 bearing: 8 mm bore, 22 mm outside diameter, 7 mm wide; SKF 608-2Z rated 3.45 kN dynamic, 1.37 kN static (123bearing); the usual skateboard wheel bearing (Wikipedia).

Precision shoulder screws: shoulder 0.013 to 0.038 mm under nominal and shoulder length 0.013 to 0.063 mm over nominal (metric), so a part of nominal size turns freely; commercial shoulder lengths are only +/-0.125 mm, so a full-width part can bind (Machine Design).
Bolt as a pivot: make the smooth (unthreaded) grip length about equal to the thickness of the parts and washers it passes through (Wikipedia, Bolt).
Printed pivots: at least 0.3 mm clearance for moving parts (Prusa); drill critical upright holes to size, and use off-the-shelf pins below 5 mm diameter (Hubs).

everyday_examples: Skateboard and inline-skate wheels, each running on two 608 ball bearings (Wikipedia, Ball bearing)
Fidget spinners, built around ball bearings (Wikipedia, Ball bearing)
The lever of a door handle turning on its spindle (Wikipedia, Revolute joint photo)
Scissors and pliers, whose two halves turn on one rivet or screw [uncertain]
guidance.when_to_use: Use a plain pivot (a bolt, shoulder screw or pin in a hole, ideally with a bushing) for levers, arms, linkages, folding parts and anything that turns slowly, occasionally or back and forth: it is cheap, compact and strong for its size (Wikipedia, Plain bearing). A shoulder screw is the neat choice when a part must turn on a bolt without being clamped (Machine Design). Use ball bearings for anything that spins continuously or fast, such as wheels, pulleys, spools, fans and drive shafts, where low friction and accurate location matter; robotics guides recommend bearings for drivetrains and high speeds and bushings for low loads or tight budgets (GM0). Add a thrust washer where a turning part would otherwise rub against a fixed face or a pin head; washers are used in rotating devices as a bearing and as a wear pad (Wikipedia, Washer (hardware)).
guidance.when_not_to_use: Don't run a plain printed pin in a printed hole fast and continuously under load: it heats and wears (see the PV limits); use a ball bearing or a bronze or plastic bushing. Don't hang a tipping load on a single ball bearing; use two spaced apart, or a turntable bearing for a wide, flat turning platform. Ball bearings that only rock back and forth over a small angle, or sit still while vibrating, suffer false brinelling (Wikipedia), so a bushing may be better there. For tiny angles with no play and no wear, use a flexure hinge; for straight-line motion, use linear guides; for a pivot that must also tilt, use a ball-and-socket joint or rod end.
guidance.environment_limits: Plastic bushings: nylon is listed for about -29 to 121 °C and acetal about -29 to 82 °C, while SAE 841 bronze is listed to about 104 °C (Wikipedia, Plain bearing table, converted from °F). Plastic bearings creep, expand with heat and soften when warm (Wikipedia, Plain bearing), and absorb moisture; igus sizes its bushings to cope with humidity up to 70% (igus). Printed PLA starts to give at about 60 °C and PETG at about 80 °C (CNC Kitchen). Ball bearings: grit and water in the lubricant greatly shorten their life, and seals help but add friction (Wikipedia, Rolling-element bearing); vibration while standing still presses the grease out (false brinelling; Wikipedia). Plain steel pins and bearings rust outdoors unless stainless or protected [uncertain].
guidance.safety_notes: Pivoting levers and arms make scissor-like pinch points [uncertain]. Spinning parts on bearings can catch hair, loose clothing or fingers. When pressing in bearings, push on the ring you are fitting rather than through the balls, and wear eye protection, because too much interference can crack a ring (NSK: excessive interference can crack the inner ring) [uncertain].
guidance.common_failures: Plain pivots: the hole wears oval and the joint gets sloppy; threads left in the hole fret the hole (Wikipedia, Bolt); dry or overloaded bushings gall and seize when lubrication fails (Wikipedia, Plain bearing); a pivot bolt that turns with the part slowly unscrews, so use a shoulder screw or a locking nut [uncertain]; thin printed pins snap (Hubs). Ball bearings: a ring fitted too loosely creeps round in its seat and wears it, and one fitted too tightly cracks or runs hot (NSK); dirt and water ruin them (Wikipedia); a single bearing under a sideways twist collapses (Wikipedia, Ball bearing). Printed parts: pockets come out too tight or too loose (Hackaday, crush ribs), and printed bearings fuse or bind unless their tolerances are calibrated (Printables 276409).
related: Clevis joint (fork-and-pin joint): a pin supported on both sides by a fork, so it is loaded in double shear
Knuckle hinge (butt hinge): a pin pivot spread along a door edge through interleaved knuckles
Turntable bearing (lazy-Susan bearing, slewing ring): a thin, wide ring bearing for platforms and tipping loads
Roller clutch (one-way bearing): a bearing that turns freely one way and locks the other
Flexure hinge: bends instead of sliding or rolling; no play and no wear, but only a small angle
Rolling-contact joint (CORE, Jacob's-ladder hinge): two curved surfaces roll on each other instead of turning on a pin
Linear guides: bushings and bearings for straight-line motion
Press fit (interference fit): how bearings and bushings are usually held in place
Retaining ring (circlip, E-clip): stops a pin or shaft sliding out
Shaft-to-hub joints (key, set screw, D-flat, clamp hub): fix a gear or wheel to the turning shaft
Mid-print embedding: trapping a bearing inside a printed part
Rod end and ball link, Ball-and-socket joint: pivots that also allow tilt
Castor: a wheel turning on an axle in a bracket, with a second, swivel bearing on top so the wheel trails behind and steers itself
Ball caster: a large ball carried on small bearing balls, so it rolls in every direction instead of turning about one axis
Split-pin paper fastener (brass paper fastener): the standard beginner pivot in paper and card, a brass pin with its legs spread behind
Cardboard construction screws and box rivets: smooth-shank rivets and plastic hinges give swinging pivot joints in cardboard
Volvelle (paper wheel chart): paper discs turning on one shared centre pivot
Glass door hinge: includes pivot hinges that clamp a glass door's top and bottom corners onto pins turning in the cabinet
